Advanced local projections: state dependence, smoothing, panels, joint inference and forecasting

Source: vignettes/lp-advanced.Rmd
lp-advanced.Rmd

This vignette covers the extensions built on top of lp(), which is defined in vignette("local-projections"): state-dependent LP (lp_state()), smooth LP (lp_smooth()), panel LP (lp_panel()), joint cross-horizon inference with sup-t bands (lp_joint(), lp_supt()) and direct forecasts (lp_forecast()). Every result has tidy() and autoplot() methods: autoplot() returns an ordinary ggplot (add layers with +) and tidy() returns a tibble with the columns horizon, response, estimate, std.error, level, conf.low, conf.high (plus state for lp_state()), ready for ggplot2 or dplyr. Variables are named with tidyselect syntax. Each section gives a definition, the intuition, an example and the pitfalls. Where a claim rests on simulation we run a small version of the simulation in the vignette and say what it does and does not show.

1. State-dependent LP: lp_state()

Definition

Let ztz_t be a switching variable (the state), standardised to z̃t=(zt−z‾)/sd(z)\tilde z_t=(z_t-\bar z)/\mathrm{sd}(z). Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012, 2013) let every coefficient of the LP depend on the state at t−1t-1 through a transition function FF: yt+h=F(z̃t−1)[αhL+βhLst+γhL′wt]+(1−F(z̃t−1))[αhH+βhHst+γhH′wt]+et+h. y_{t+h}=F(\tilde z_{t-1})\big[\alpha^L_h+\beta^L_h s_t+\gamma^{L\prime}_h w_t\big] +\big(1-F(\tilde z_{t-1})\big)\big[\alpha^H_h+\beta^H_h s_t+\gamma^{H\prime}_h w_t\big]+e_{t+h}. Two transitions are available:

  • transition = "logistic": F(z̃)=1/(1+exp⁡{γ(z̃−c)})F(\tilde z)=1/(1+\exp\{\gamma(\tilde z-c)\}) with smoothness gamma and cutoff cutoff (or low_share). F→1F\to 1 when zz is well below cc, so “low” is the state in which the switching variable is low;
  • transition = "binary": F=1{z̃t−1<c}F=1\{\tilde z_{t-1}<c\}.

The response is βhL\beta^L_h in the low state and βhH\beta^H_h in the high state. The function estimates both in one regression per horizon (C++ engine), reports βhL−βhH\beta^L_h-\beta^H_h (diff = low - high) with a HAC tt-test at each horizon and a joint Wald test over horizons.

Calibration. γ\gamma and cc are not estimated. Auerbach and Gorodnichenko use γ=1.5\gamma=1.5 and a cutoff such that the low state has roughly 20% weight; low_share = 0.2 sets cc to that quantile. hp_lambda = 1600 replaces the raw state by its Hodrick-Prescott cycle (quarterly data).

Timing. The state enters lagged one period, F(z̃t−1)F(\tilde z_{t-1}), so that the shock cannot move the state it is being interacted with within the same period. This matches Auerbach and Gorodnichenko; it is a convention, and a state that responds to the shock with a lag still contaminates the comparison at longer horizons.

Intuition

Fiscal and monetary effects are often thought to differ across the cycle. A nonlinear VAR would impose how the state evolves; the LP lets the response at each horizon be state-specific and does not model state transitions, so the state may change over the horizon. The price is variance: each state uses only the observations weighted by FF or 1−F1-F.

Example

We ask whether the response to a one-point rate rise differs when unemployment is low or high, using a smooth transition with 30% of the weight in the low-unemployment state:

st <- lp_state(yraw, rate, unemp, horizon = 12, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp),
               gamma = 3, low_share = 0.3, responses = c(infl, unemp))
st
#> <lp_state> contemporaneous timing, logistic transition, shock 'rate', horizons 0..12; low-state share 0.29
#> Joint test of equal responses across states (Wald):
#>         stat df     p
#> infl  57.775 12 0.000
#> unemp 20.513 12 0.058
glance(st)                      # includes the cutoff and share_low
#> # A tibble: 1 × 9
#>   shock horizon  lags timing          transition cutoff share_low  nobs   wald_p
#>   <chr>   <int> <int> <chr>           <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 rate       12     2 contemporaneous logistic   -0.503     0.294   213  5.73e-8
h <- c(2, 5, 9, 13)                              # rows for horizons 1, 4, 8, 12
round(cbind(low = st$estimate[h, "infl", "low"], high = st$estimate[h, "infl", "high"],
            diff = st$estimate[h, "infl", "diff"], p = st$pvalue[h, "infl"]), 3)
#>      low   high  diff     p
#> 1  0.116 -0.096 0.212 0.058
#> 4  0.522 -0.100 0.622 0.070
#> 8  0.980 -0.332 1.312 0.015
#> 12 0.178 -0.657 0.835 0.053
autoplot(st)                    # low and high state overlaid

The difference between the two states, with its own bands, is autoplot(st, type = "diff"):

autoplot(st, type = "diff") + labs(title = "Low minus high unemployment state")

The first panel of the plot (inflation) shows the “low unemployment” response well above the “high unemployment” one at medium horizons, and the Wald test rejects equality for inflation at conventional levels. For unemployment the joint test is borderline. These are descriptive findings from one sample, not evidence of a causal asymmetry: the state is calibrated, the rate is identified only by the recursive ordering, and the effective sample in the low state is small.

The calibration matters. The same specification with different smoothness and low-state shares gives joint Wald pp-values for unemployment that range widely:

pv <- sapply(c(0.2, 0.5), function(q) sapply(c(1.5, 3, 10), function(g)
  lp_state(yraw, rate, unemp, 8, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp), gamma = g, low_share = q,
           responses = unemp)$wald[1, "p"]))
dimnames(pv) <- list(gamma = c(1.5, 3, 10), low_share = c(0.2, 0.5))
round(pv, 3)
#>      low_share
#> gamma   0.2   0.5
#>   1.5 0.274 0.119
#>   3   0.510 0.112
#>   10  0.403 0.026

A conclusion that flips between “reject” and “do not reject” across reasonable calibrations should be reported as such.

Convention check against lpirfs::lp_nl

With timing = "lagged" the function replicates the convention of lpirfs::lp_nl(): the regressors are lags of yy interacted with the state, no contemporaneous terms, and the horizon-hh response is the coefficient on yt−1y_{t-1} in the equation for yt+h−1y_{t+h-1} multiplied by a column of the Cholesky impact matrix of a linear VAR (standard-deviation shock for shock_type = 0). The impact response (h=0h=0) is that column in both states. Bands here are normal quantiles at level, whereas lpirfs uses a user multiplier on the coefficient-wise standard errors, and lpirfs uses a common constant, so set state_const = FALSE to compare.

zz <- as.numeric(scale(yraw$unemp))
ref <- lpirfs::lp_nl(as.data.frame(yraw), lags_endog_lin = 2, lags_endog_nl = 2, trend = 0,
                     shock_type = 0, confint = 1, hor = 8, switching = zz, use_hp = 0,
                     lambda = 1600, gamma = 3, use_nw = TRUE, num_cores = 1)
me <- lp_state(yraw, shock = rate, state = unemp, horizon = 8, lags = 2, timing = "lagged",
               lags_lin = 2, shock_type = 0, gamma = 3, state_const = FALSE)
# lpirfs state 1 = high, state 2 = low (F -> 1 in the low state)
c(high = max(abs(me$estimate[, , "high"] - t(ref$irf_s1_mean[, , 3]))),
  low  = max(abs(me$estimate[, , "low"]  - t(ref$irf_s2_mean[, , 3]))))
#>         high          low 
#> 1.213196e-13 1.543765e-13

The point estimates agree to numerical precision. The "contemporaneous" default is a different (shock-regression) specification: do not compare its numbers with lp_nl directly.

Pitfalls

  • γ\gamma and cc are calibrated, not estimated. Report sensitivity (above).
  • With transition = "binary" one regime may have few observations; check share_low.
  • The difference test has low power at long horizons with persistent states.
  • The state must be (close to) exogenous to the shock beyond one lag.
  • Not all options of lpirfs::lp_nl carry over; see the comparison above.

2. Smooth LP: lp_smooth()

Definition

Raw LP estimates are noisy and jagged because each horizon is a separate regression. Barnichon and Brownlees (2019) impose that the response is a smooth function of the horizon, β(h)=∑j=1JθjBj(h)\beta(h)=\sum_{j=1}^J\theta_jB_j(h) with a B-spline basis (nbasis, default min⁡(H+1,8)\min(H+1,8); cubic by default) and estimate all horizons jointly by penalised least squares: θ̂=arg⁡minθ∑h=0H∑t(ỹt+h−∑jθjBj(h)s̃t,h)2+λθ′Dr′Drθ, \hat\theta=\arg\min_\theta\sum_{h=0}^{H}\sum_t\Big(\tilde y_{t+h}-\sum_j\theta_jB_j(h)\tilde s_{t,h}\Big)^2+\lambda\,\theta'D_r'D_r\theta, where tildes denote residuals from the horizon-specific regression on the controls (Frisch-Waugh) and DrD_r is the rr-th order difference matrix (Eilers and Marx’s P-spline penalty, penalty_order = 2). As λ→∞\lambda\to\infty the response tends to a polynomial of degree r−1r-1. The penalty λ\lambda is chosen by KK-fold cross-validation over contiguous blocks of time (nfolds), so serial dependence is not broken by random splits. Standard errors use the HAC sandwich (A+λP)−1Ω̂(A+λP)−1(A+\lambda P)^{-1}\hat\Omega(A+\lambda P)^{-1} with Newey-West truncation H + 1 on the scores summed over horizons.

Intuition

Theory suggests responses are smooth. Pooling neighbouring horizons trades a small bias for a large variance reduction, which places smooth LP between unrestricted LP and a parametric VAR in the bias-variance trade-off of vignette("local-projections").

Example 

sm <- lp_smooth(yraw, shock = rate, response = unemp, horizon = 16, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp))
c(lambda = sm$lambda, edf = sm$edf)
#>     lambda        edf 
#> 106.623109   3.271681
round(cbind(smooth = sm$estimate[, 1], raw = sm$lp, se_smooth = sm$se[, 1], se_raw = sm$lp_se)[c(2, 5, 9, 13, 17), ], 3)
#>    smooth    raw se_smooth se_raw
#> 1  -0.035 -0.030     0.059  0.045
#> 4   0.044  0.028     0.055  0.081
#> 8   0.144  0.194     0.056  0.066
#> 12  0.156  0.149     0.083  0.101
#> 16  0.091  0.071     0.125  0.118
autoplot(sm) + labs(title = "rate -> unemp: smooth LP (90% band) versus raw LP")

The CV choice of λ\lambda is stored in sm$cv (a grid of 21 values scaled by tr(A)/J\mathrm{tr}(A)/J, from 10−410^{-4} to 10410^{4}); a CV curve that is flat or minimised at an edge of the grid is a warning to supply lambda and nbasis yourself.

Monte Carlo evidence

A VAR(1) with T=200T=200 and a recursive identification; we compare the mean squared error of the response path of yy to a unit impulse in xx, for raw and smooth LP, and the pointwise coverage of the nominal 90% band (100 replications, so figures carry Monte Carlo error of a few percentage points on coverage).

A <- matrix(c(0.6, 0.2, 0, 0.5), 2, 2); Pc <- t(chol(matrix(c(1, .3, .3, 1), 2)))
Ht <- 12
truth <- sapply(0:Ht, function(h) { M <- diag(2); for (i in seq_len(h)) M <- A %*% M; (M %*% Pc[, 1] / Pc[1, 1])[2] })
sim2 <- function(n = 250, burn = 50) {
  e <- matrix(rnorm(2 * n), n) %*% t(Pc); Y <- matrix(0, n, 2)
  for (t in 2:n) Y[t, ] <- A %*% Y[t - 1, ] + e[t, ]
  Y <- Y[-seq_len(burn), ]; colnames(Y) <- c("x", "y"); Y
}
R <- 100; out <- matrix(0, R, 4, dimnames = list(NULL, c("mse_raw", "mse_smooth", "cov_raw", "cov_smooth")))
for (r in seq_len(R)) {
  Y <- sim2()
  f <- lp(Y, x, Ht, lags = 2, responses = y); s <- lp_smooth(Y, x, y, Ht, lags = 2)
  out[r, ] <- c(mean((f$estimate[, 1] - truth)^2), mean((s$estimate[, 1] - truth)^2),
                mean(truth >= f$bands[, 1, 1] & truth <= f$bands[, 1, 4]),
                mean(truth >= s$bands[, 1, 1] & truth <= s$bands[, 1, 4]))
}
m <- colMeans(out)
round(c(m, mse_ratio = unname(m["mse_smooth"] / m["mse_raw"])), 3)
#>    mse_raw mse_smooth    cov_raw cov_smooth  mse_ratio 
#>      0.008      0.005      0.872      0.772      0.651

Smoothing reduces the mean squared error of the response path to roughly two thirds of the raw LP’s (a ratio of about 0.65 to 0.67 in this run and in larger ones). The coverage columns show the limitation: the smooth LP’s pointwise bands cover less than the raw LP’s. They are conditional on the selected λ\lambda and ignore both the smoothing bias and the uncertainty from choosing λ\lambda by cross-validation. Use smooth LP for point estimates and shape, and treat its bands as optimistic.

Pitfalls

  • Sharp features (an impact jump, a sudden reversal) are smoothed away; the horizon-0 value is part of the smooth curve, not pinned at its known value.
  • One response at a time (response); cumulative = TRUE cumulates the response.
  • Bands ignore the selection of λ\lambda (see above). sm$vcov is compatible with lp_supt(), with the same caveat.
  • The default basis has at most 8 functions; with a long horizon increase nbasis.

3. Panel LP: lp_panel()

Definition

For a panel (i,t)(i,t) and each horizon, yi,t+h=αi,h+δt,h+βhsit+∑l=1L(ϕl,hyi,t−l+ψl,hsi,t−l)+κh′xit+ei,t+h. y_{i,t+h}=\alpha_{i,h}+\delta_{t,h}+\beta_hs_{it}+\sum_{l=1}^{L}\big(\phi_{l,h}y_{i,t-l}+\psi_{l,h}s_{i,t-l}\big)+\kappa_h'x_{it}+e_{i,t+h}. fe chooses unit effects αi\alpha_i, time effects δt\delta_t, both ("twoway", default) or none. Estimation is by within transformation (alternating projections for unbalanced two-way panels, so no dummy matrix is built) and standard errors cluster on the unit (cluster = "unit") or on time, with the Stata-type small-sample factor GG−1n−1n−k\frac{G}{G-1}\frac{n-1}{n-k}, kk counting the regressors and the absorbed effects. Clustering is what allows for the MA(hh) serial correlation of the residuals within a unit. The cross-horizon cluster covariance is returned in $vcov for lp_supt().

Intuition

Panels provide identification and power. Unit effects remove time-invariant heterogeneity; time effects remove shocks common to all units, so βh\beta_h is identified from cross-sectional differences in exposure to ss. The cost is interpretation: with time effects the estimate is a relative effect (units with more of the shock versus fewer) and the aggregate effect is absorbed.

Example: a simulated panel

Forty units, 50 periods. The shock has a unit-specific mean and a common component, and the outcome has unit effects and a common time shock, so pooled OLS is biased. The true response is 0.5×0.7h0.5\times0.7^h.

set.seed(5); N <- 40; Tn <- 50
ft <- rnorm(Tn); mu <- rnorm(N)                       # common time shock; unit effects
d <- expand.grid(t = 1:Tn, id = 1:N)
d$s <- 0.5 * mu[d$id] + 0.5 * ft[d$t] + rnorm(nrow(d))
d$y <- 0
for (i in 1:N) {
  ix <- which(d$id == i); yy <- 0
  for (k in seq_along(ix)) { yy <- 0.7 * yy + 0.5 * d$s[ix[k]] + mu[i] + ft[k] + rnorm(1); d$y[ix[k]] <- yy }
}
hs <- c(0, 2, 4, 8)
res <- sapply(c(none = "none", unit = "unit", time = "time", twoway = "twoway"),
              function(f) lp_panel(d, y, s, id, t, horizon = 8, lags = 1, fe = f)$estimate[hs + 1])
round(cbind(res, truth = 0.5 * 0.7^hs), 3)
#>       none  unit  time twoway truth
#> [1,] 1.007 0.949 0.603  0.529 0.500
#> [2,] 0.841 0.581 0.472  0.271 0.245
#> [3,] 0.515 0.141 0.406  0.127 0.120
#> [4,] 0.403 0.057 0.336  0.020 0.029

Only the two-way specification recovers the truth; omitting either effect leaves bias at every horizon. Now the two-way fit with its bands:

pn <- lp_panel(d, y, s, id, t, horizon = 8, lags = 1)
pn$nclusters[1]
#> [1] 40
round(cbind(estimate = pn$estimate[, 1], se = pn$se[, 1], truth = 0.5 * 0.7^(0:8))[c(1, 3, 5, 9), ], 3)
#>   estimate    se truth
#> 0    0.529 0.021 0.500
#> 2    0.271 0.036 0.245
#> 4    0.127 0.051 0.120
#> 8    0.020 0.032 0.029
autoplot(pn) +
  geom_line(aes(y = truth, linetype = "truth"), data = data.frame(horizon = 0:8, truth = 0.5 * 0.7^(0:8))) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = "dashed", name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Panel LP, two-way fixed effects")

The estimates are within about one standard error of the truth at the horizons shown. Note the small shortfall at h=8h=8: with unit effects and lagged outcomes among the controls the within transformation brings in a small-TT (Nickell-type) bias of order 1/T1/T times the cumulated response, which is why the pitfall below recommends long panels.

Pitfalls

  • Fixed effects with lagged dependent variables give Nickell bias when TT is small; use long panels or drop the y lags.
  • With few clusters (fewer than about 30) cluster-robust bands are too narrow.
  • With time effects the estimate is relative; heterogeneous responses are averaged with variance weights.
  • time must be regularly spaced; duplicated (unit, time) pairs are an error.

4. Joint inference and sup-t bands: lp_joint(), lp_supt()

Definition

LP estimates at neighbouring horizons are built from overlapping data and are strongly correlated, so a pointwise band says little about the whole path. lp_joint() runs the same regressions as lp() and in addition returns, for each response, the (H+1)×(H+1)(H+1)\times(H+1) covariance matrix of (β̂0,…,β̂H)′(\hat\beta_0,\dots,\hat\beta_H)': Cov̂(β̂h,β̂h′)=∑l=−LLwl∑tqt,hêt+hqt−l,h′êt−l+h′,wl=1−|l|L+1, \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(\hat\beta_h,\hat\beta_{h'})=\sum_{l=-L}^{L}w_l\sum_t q_{t,h}\hat e_{t+h}\,q_{t-l,h'}\hat e_{t-l+h'},\qquad w_l=1-\frac{|l|}{L+1}, with L=max⁡(h,h′)+1L=\max(h,h')+1 or a common nw_lag. Its diagonal reproduces the standard errors of lp(). lp_supt() then builds the sup-t band of Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller (2019): β̂h±ĉ1−ασ̂h\hat\beta_h\pm\hat c_{1-\alpha}\hat\sigma_h with ĉ1−α\hat c_{1-\alpha} the (1−α)(1-\alpha)-quantile of max⁡h|zh|\max_h|z_h|, z∼N(0,R̂)z\sim N(0,\hat R), where R̂\hat R is the correlation matrix implied by the joint covariance (simulated, nsim draws). It covers the whole path with probability 1−α1-\alpha asymptotically, is narrower than Bonferroni and is never narrower than the pointwise band.

Example 

j <- lp_joint(yraw, shock = rate, horizon = 16, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp), responses = unemp)
max(abs(sqrt(diag(j$vcov[[1]])) - j$se[, 1]))      # diagonal = lp() standard errors
#> [1] 6.938894e-17
b <- lp_supt(j, level = 0.9, seed = 1)
attr(b, "crit")                                    # sup-t critical value (pointwise: 1.645)
#>    unemp 
#> 2.458333
b[c(2, 5, 9, 13, 17), c("horizon", "estimate", "pw_low", "pw_high", "conf.low", "conf.high")] |>
  as.data.frame() |> round(3)
#>   horizon estimate pw_low pw_high conf.low conf.high
#> 1       1   -0.030 -0.103   0.044   -0.140     0.081
#> 2       4    0.028 -0.105   0.161   -0.170     0.227
#> 3       8    0.194  0.086   0.302    0.032     0.355
#> 4      12    0.149 -0.017   0.314   -0.099     0.396
#> 5      16    0.071 -0.123   0.265   -0.219     0.361

lp_supt() returns a tibble with columns response, horizon, estimate, std.error, pw_low, pw_high (pointwise) and conf.low, conf.high (sup-t). autoplot() draws both bands, and tidy() stacks them (a band column) for your own plots:

autoplot(b) + labs(title = "rate -> unemp: pointwise and sup-t 90% bands")

The sup-t critical value is about 2.5, between the pointwise 1.645 and the Bonferroni value of roughly 3 for 17 horizons. Horizons with zero variance (the normalised impact response) are ignored. You can also use the joint covariance for a Wald test that the whole response is zero.

How reliable are sup-t bands in finite samples? (honest answer: not very)

The sup-t result is asymptotic and relies on a good joint covariance. We simulate the VAR(1) of the previous section with T=200T=200 and measure the share of replications in which the entire true path (h=0,…,12h=0,\dots,12) lies inside a nominal 90% band. Two estimators: the default Newey-West covariance with two lags, and lag augmentation (one lag plus an extra lag, HC covariance). 300 replications; coverage carries Monte Carlo error of about ±0.02\pm0.02.

cover_path <- function(la, lg, R = 300) {
  set.seed(42); hit <- matrix(0, R, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("pointwise", "sup-t")))
  for (r in seq_len(R)) {
    Y <- sim2()
    bb <- lp_supt(lp_joint(Y, x, Ht, lags = lg, responses = y, lag_augment = la), 0.9, nsim = 2000, seed = r)
    hit[r, ] <- c(all(truth >= bb$pw_low & truth <= bb$pw_high), all(truth >= bb$conf.low & truth <= bb$conf.high))
  }
  colMeans(hit)
}
round(rbind(`Newey-West (lags = 2)` = cover_path(FALSE, 2), `lag-augmented (lags = 1 + 1)` = cover_path(TRUE, 1)), 2)
#>                              pointwise sup-t
#> Newey-West (lags = 2)             0.24  0.78
#> lag-augmented (lags = 1 + 1)      0.33  0.84

Pointwise bands cover the whole path in only a quarter to a third of the replications, which is what one expects from 13 correlated 90% intervals. Sup-t bands do much better but fall short of the 0.90 target: about 0.78 with Newey-West and about 0.84 with lag augmentation. The HAC covariance is estimated imprecisely at long horizons in a sample of 200, so the critical value is too small. The shortfall is a finite-sample property of HAC and HC inference for LP and is not specific to lp_supt().

Recommendation. Lag augmentation (lag_augment = TRUE) helps somewhat (0.84 against 0.78 at a nominal 0.90) but does not close the gap; for pointwise coverage at long horizons it is not a visible improvement (vignette("local-projections")). Treat sup-t coverage as approximate, and do not read “the band excludes zero at every horizon” as a 90% statement.

Pitfalls

  • With the default horizon-specific bandwidth the joint covariance is not guaranteed positive semi-definite:
c(default = min(eigen(j$vcov[[1]])$values),
  common_nw_lag = min(eigen(lp_joint(yraw, rate, 16, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp), responses = unemp,
                                     nw_lag = 17)$vcov[[1]])$values))
#>       default common_nw_lag 
#> -8.774400e-05  1.728649e-28

The default has a (slightly) negative smallest eigenvalue; with a common nw_lag the matrix is positive semi-definite (the remaining zero eigenvalue belongs to the normalised horizon 0). Pass a common nw_lag if you need to invert it. * lp_supt() also accepts lp_smooth() and lp_panel() objects (each has $vcov), with the caveats of their own sections. * Highly persistent data make HAC covariances unreliable at long horizons.

5. Direct multi-step forecasts: lp_forecast()

Definition

For each h=1,…,Hh=1,\dots,H regress yt+hy_{t+h} on xt=(1,yt′,…,yt−p+1′)′x_t=(1,y_t',\dots,y_{t-p+1}')' and forecast ŷT+h=xT′B̂h\hat y_{T+h}=x_T'\hat B_h. The forecast standard error is σ̂h1+xT′(Xh′Xh)−1xT\hat\sigma_h\sqrt{1+x_T'(X_h'X_h)^{-1}x_T} (the unconditional residual variance, which is what matters for the forecast error even though the residual is MA(h−1h-1)). Bands are normal quantiles at level.

Intuition

Iterated (VAR) forecasts are efficient if the VAR is correctly specified but compound misspecification with the horizon; direct forecasts estimate each horizon’s conditional mean separately, which is robust to misspecification but noisier (Marcellino, Stock and Watson, 2006). At h=1h=1 the two coincide exactly.

Example 

fl <- lp_forecast(yraw, horizon = 4, lags = 2)
fv <- forecast(varm(yraw, 2), h = 4, ci = "none")
round(rbind(`direct h=1` = fl$mean[1, ], `iterated h=1` = fv$mean[1, ],
            `direct h=4` = fl$mean[4, ], `iterated h=4` = fv$mean[4, ]), 3)
#>               infl unemp  rate
#> direct h=1   2.721 4.921 4.620
#> iterated h=1 2.721 4.921 4.620
#> direct h=4   2.771 5.319 4.204
#> iterated h=4 2.656 5.232 4.251
round(fl$se, 3)
#>    infl unemp  rate
#> 1 0.311 0.335 0.776
#> 2 0.563 0.546 1.083
#> 3 0.799 0.714 1.244
#> 4 1.033 0.811 1.453
autoplot(fl)

The direct and iterated forecasts coincide at h=1h=1 and differ slightly at h=4h=4. The standard errors grow with the horizon. They are plug-in errors that ignore any serial correlation across horizons.

Pitfalls

  • Forecasts at different horizons are not constrained to be consistent with each other and can be jagged.
  • Direct forecasts need a long sample; for a short sample or many variables use a BVAR (vignette("bayesian-var")).
  • Bands are Gaussian; there is no density forecast.
